package.name: cross-cultural-dishonesty-study-reports-of-roll-outcomes-die-task
package.author: Heather Mann, Ximena Garcia-Rada, Lars Hornuf, Juan Tafurt, Dan Ariely
package.notes: Data were collected from 10 participant samples from the following five countries: China, Colombia, Germany, Portugal, and USA.  In each country, we administered the die task to a sample of student participants (in universities) and a sample of participants from the general public (in coffee shops).  The task, adapted from Jiang (2013), was administered on iPads and was used assessed dishonesty.  Participants roll a (virtual) six-sided die, and each time, before rolling, were asked to select a side, either top or bottom, and keep it in mind.  They were instructed that they would earn a fixed amount of money (the equivalent of 10 cents USD) for every dot on the chosen side.  Participants then rolled the die and viewed the outcome, which displayed the number of dots on top and bottom.  They were then asked to report which side they had chosen.  In our study, participants repeated this task for 20 trials.  The HRProp variable represents the proportion of times that a participant selected the side with more favorable earnings after viewing the outcome.  These data were collected from Feb 2013-March 2014.
package.title: Cross-cultural dishonesty study - Reports of roll outcomes die task

package.name: predictions-of-dishonesty-on-die-task-administered-across-countries
package.author: Heather Mann, Ximena Garcia-Rada, Lars Hornuf, Juan Tafurt, Dan Ariely
package.notes: We administered a die task to ten participant samples across five countries: China, Colombia, Germany, Portugal, and USA.  In each country, the task was administered on iPads to a sample of students (at universities) and a sample of the general public (in coffee shops).  This study asked online samples of participants from the same five countries to predict the extent to which favourable rolls were reported on the die task, on a response scale ranging from 50 (perfectly honest) to 100 (perfectly dishonest).  The subjects in this study predicted the extent of dishonesty for each of the ten samples in our cross-cultural dishonesty study.
package.title: Predictions of dishonesty on die task administered across countries

package.name: lying-tendencies-in-socially-connected-pairs
package.author: Heather Mann
package.notes: This data was collected from participants who took a survey as part of a Massive Open Online Course, and friends or relatives of these students who received a survey invitation via email.  Using multiple regression analyses, we explored whether participants who were connected to one another exhibited similar self-reported lying tendencies.
package.title: Lying Tendencies in Socially-Connected Pairs
